# Baseline Balance

A finite randomized sample can show baseline differences by chance. Such differences may affect precision, but their existence alone does not establish a broken assignment procedure. Audit the actual allocation mechanism and report important baseline characteristics. Plan justified adjustment or stratification prospectively where possible. Do not repeatedly rerandomize until an attractive result appears without defining and accounting for that design.

label.rationale: Treats a probabilistic design property as exact matching.

# Crossover Carryover

Crossover designs compare conditions within the same unit, but earlier exposure may influence later outcomes. Counterbalancing order helps with some order effects and does not by itself remove every carryover mechanism. Decide whether a justified washout is possible and whether the intended estimand remains meaningful. Record period and sequence, and test the design on tasks where the unit can genuinely return to the relevant starting condition.

label.rationale: Assumes within-unit comparison erases temporal dependence.

unit.skip_condition: Explain why removing participants who disappear after assignment can bias an arm comparison.

state.explanation: Once randomization happens, any later removal is harmless because the original random process permanently guarantees comparable survivors.

document:
# Attrition Comparison

Follow-up loss can differ between experiment arms or depend on results that would have been observed. Dropping missing units without examining this mechanism can undermine the original comparison. Track every assigned unit, report losses and their reasons, and specify missing-data handling prospectively. Sensitivity analyses can show dependence on assumptions; they do not recover unobserved outcomes with certainty.

label.rationale: Assumes the initial assignment protects an arbitrarily selected later subset.

unit.skip_condition: Explain why the randomization unit determines which observations can be treated as independently assigned.

document:
# Assignment Unit

An experiment assigns treatment to a defined unit, which may be a person, task, machine or entire group. Multiple observations inside that unit do not create additional independent assignments. Preserve assignment identifiers in collected data and plan an analysis that respects their grouping. Reporting many measurements without their dependence structure can make uncertainty appear smaller than the design supports.

label.rationale: Mistakes repeated observations within one assignment for independent assignments.

# Backpressure

Streaming describes incremental processing, not an automatic bound on every queue. A fast decompressor can create expanded output faster than a downstream writer or parser consumes it. Use bounded buffers and propagate backpressure through the pipeline. Measure queued decoded bytes under a deliberately slow consumer, and make interruption or limit failures visible instead of silently dropping output.

label.rationale: Assumes a streaming interface alone guarantees bounded memory.

Define whether the application accepts one member, several members or trailing data. Verify how much input was consumed and whether every accepted member completed. A successful first-member decode is not automatically evidence that the whole uploaded object followed the intended framing contract.

label.rationale: Assumes universal concatenation behavior across formats and decoders.

# Flush Versus Finish

Compression APIs often distinguish flushing buffered output from finishing a stream. Flush modes can make current data available without writing the final framing information. Use the documented finalization operation and propagate its errors before reporting success. Test empty and very short payloads as well as ordinary files, since omitted trailers can be easy to miss when a decoder returns partial output early.

label.rationale: Distinguishes output availability from format completion.

state.explanation: Decoded output can accumulate faster than its consumer processes it, so bounded buffering and paused input keep expansion from creating unbounded queued output.

document:
# Backpressure

Streaming describes incremental processing, not an automatic bound on every queue. A fast decompressor can create expanded output faster than a downstream writer or parser consumes it. Use bounded buffers and propagate backpressure through the pipeline. Measure queued decoded bytes under a deliberately slow consumer, and make interruption or limit failures visible instead of silently dropping output.

label.rationale: Connects rate imbalance to buffering and a concrete flow-control response.

unit.skip_condition: Explain why limiting compressed input bytes alone does not bound decompressed output memory.

state.explanation: A small compressed file always needs less memory than a large one, so checking its file size is a sufficient decompression limit.

document:
# Expanded Size

Compression ratios vary with content. A compact encoded stream can describe a much larger output, so an input-size check does not by itself bound allocation or disk use. Apply output and work limits during decoding, before materializing an unlimited result. If the limit is reached, retain a distinct failure status rather than presenting the truncated output as a successfully decoded complete object.

label.rationale: Assumes compressed size directly bounds expanded size.

state.explanation: Randomization prevents assessors from favoring an arm, so revealing treatment labels cannot affect subjective scoring.

document:
# Measurement Blinding

Randomization controls assignment, not every later measurement decision. When an assessor knows the arm, borderline outcomes can be interpreted differently. Blind assessors where feasible, provide prospective acceptance criteria and record adjudication. When blinding is impossible, disclose that limitation and use objective measurements where they answer the question. Agreement with an expected result is not evidence that an unblinded judgment was unbiased.

label.rationale: Assumes random allocation controls the assessor's later judgment.

# Member Framing

Some compressed formats allow multiple members, while decoder APIs differ in how they expose member boundaries and remaining input. Define whether the application accepts one member, several members or trailing data. Verify how much input was consumed and whether every accepted member completed. A successful first-member decode is not automatically evidence that the whole uploaded object followed the intended framing contract.

label.rationale: Recognizes both member handling and complete-input validation.

# Intention To Treat

Intention-to-treat analysis retains units in their assigned groups even when adherence differs. This preserves the assigned-policy comparison under the design's assumptions, but does not automatically estimate the effect of everyone following the intervention perfectly. Describe adherence separately and state the estimand. Analyses based on received treatment may answer other questions while requiring additional assumptions about selection into adherence.

label.rationale: Defines the assignment-based comparison and limits its interpretation.

# Allocation Concealment

Generating a random assignment sequence and concealing it are different design tasks. Knowledge of upcoming assignments can influence enrollment or task inclusion, even when the sequence itself was random. Keep future assignments unavailable to anyone who can select incoming units until eligibility is settled. Record exceptions and distinguish this protection from blinding outcomes after assignment.

label.rationale: Identifies selection before allocation as the relevant bias mechanism.

state.explanation: Exposure in the first period may affect outcomes in the second, so changing the label alone does not reset the unit; allow justified washout or account for persistent effects.

document:
# Crossover Carryover

Crossover designs compare conditions within the same unit, but earlier exposure may influence later outcomes. Counterbalancing order helps with some order effects and does not by itself remove every carryover mechanism. Decide whether a justified washout is possible and whether the intended estimand remains meaningful. Record period and sequence, and test the design on tasks where the unit can genuinely return to the relevant starting condition.

label.rationale: Describes persistent exposure and its consequence for the later comparison.

unit.skip_condition: Explain why a compression checksum does not establish who produced a stream.

state.explanation: An accidental-corruption checksum can be recomputed by anyone changing the contents, so it checks consistency rather than authenticated origin.

document:
# Checksum Authenticity

Checksums embedded in compressed formats help detect accidental damage and some decoding mistakes. They do not generally authenticate a producer or prevent deliberate replacement of both content and checksum. Use the application's authenticated integrity mechanism when provenance matters. Verify checksum handling for corruption detection while keeping the result separate from any signature or authenticated-channel verification.

label.rationale: Distinguishes integrity against accidents from authentication against deliberate modification.

state.explanation: A decoder may emit earlier output before discovering a missing footer or later corruption, so success requires its final completion and integrity status.

# Truncated Output

Streaming decoders can produce valid prefixes before they discover an incomplete or damaged suffix. Applications must inspect the final decoding status and required integrity checks before treating the entire object as valid. Decide explicitly whether partial output has a separate use, and label it accordingly. Tests should truncate the stream at several positions, including after most of the useful payload has already been emitted.

label.rationale: Identifies delayed detection and the requirement for a final status.

unit.skip_condition: Explain why choosing the most favorable outcome after measuring many outcomes weakens an ordinary single-outcome inference.

state.explanation: Measuring more outcomes can only add evidence; reporting whichever looks strongest retains the same single-outcome interpretation.

document:
# Outcome Selection

Before collection, distinguish primary outcomes from secondary or exploratory outcomes. Selecting the strongest-looking result from a large set is itself part of the analysis and changes the interpretation of an ordinary isolated threshold. Report what was measured and how selections were made. Exploratory findings can motivate a new experiment with a prospectively chosen outcome rather than being relabeled as the original test.

label.rationale: Ignores that selecting an extreme result affects its chance behavior.
